note: Where each answer comes from in law, and why it matters, in plain words. Keyed by id; rules.json, requirements.json and the screening questions point at these ids. 'says' is what the law requires, as a person would put it; 'why' is what goes wrong for people if it's ignored. Links go to the legislation itself; the ICO and DfE links elsewhere are the guidance on top.

art5.name: The principles
art5.says: Use personal data fairly and openly, for a clear reason, keep it to what you need, keep it accurate, don't keep it longer than needed, and keep it safe.
art5.why: Every other rule hangs off this one. Using more data than the job needs, or for a new reason nobody was told about, is where most trouble starts.

art6.name: Lawful basis
art6.says: You need one of six legal reasons before you use personal data at all: it's part of a public task, the law requires it, a contract needs it, the person consented, it's in a legitimate interest, or it protects someone's life.
art6.why: Without a basis nothing else can make the use lawful. For a school or college most things rest on 'public task', not consent.

art7.name: Conditions for consent
art7.says: Consent only counts if it's freely given, specific, informed, and as easy to withdraw as to give.
art7.why: Students and staff can't freely say no to the organisation that teaches or employs them, so consent usually isn't valid for them.

art9.name: Special category data
art9.says: Health, ethnicity, religion, sexual orientation, union membership, biometrics and genetics are off limits unless a specific extra condition applies. Criminal data (Art. 10) is treated the same way.
art9.why: A leak of this kind of data can cause real harm: discrimination, embarrassment, danger. That's why it stays inside the organisation.

art13.name: Telling people
art13.says: People must be told what you do with their data, in plain words, at the time you collect it or soon after you get it from someone else.
art13.why: If people don't know, they can't object, correct it, or trust you. Usually this is a line in the privacy notice.

art15.name: People's rights
art15.says: People can ask to see their data, have it corrected or deleted, object to its use, and not be subject to important decisions made by a machine alone.
art15.why: If a tool makes any of these impossible, that's a flaw in the design, not a risk to balance.

art22.name: Automated decisions
art22.says: Decisions with a serious effect on someone can't be made by a machine alone, unless specific conditions are met, and the person must be able to get a human to look again.
art22.why: An automatic fail, referral or block with nobody checking it is exactly what this article exists to stop.

art28.name: Processors and contracts
art28.says: A company that handles data for you must be bound by a written contract with set terms: act only on your instructions, keep it secure, help with rights requests, delete or return it at the end, and use other companies only with your permission.
art28.why: Without the contract you have no hold over what the company does with the data. 'On file' means this contract exists and covers this use.

art26.name: Joint controllers
art26.says: When two organisations decide together why and how data is used, they must agree in writing who does what, and tell people.
art26.why: A partner who decides things with you isn't a supplier; you need a sharing agreement, not a processor contract.

art30.name: Record of processing
art30.says: Organisations must keep a register of what personal data they use, why, who sees it, where it goes and how long it's kept.
art30.why: Anything not in the register is invisible to the people responsible for it. One line is all it takes.

art32.name: Security
art32.says: Data must be protected with measures that fit the risk: access control, encryption where it makes sense, resilience, and testing.
art32.why: This is where the IT questions come from: who can log in, where it's hosted, what happens if it breaks.

art35.name: Data protection impact assessment
art35.says: Before starting anything likely to be high risk for people, you must assess the risks and what you'll do about them. New technology, profiling, monitoring, sensitive data and children's data are the usual triggers.
art35.why: A DPIA is how you find the problem before it finds you. The screening questions here come from Art. 35(3) and the ICO's list of what counts as high risk.

art36.name: Consulting the ICO
art36.says: If a DPIA shows a high risk you can't reduce, you must consult the ICO before you start.
art36.why: This is the only point where the law itself says stop. The ICO can advise, warn, or ban the processing.

art44.name: Data leaving the UK
art44.says: Personal data can only go to another country if that country is approved (adequacy), or a recognised safeguard is in place, such as the UK's International Data Transfer Agreement or addendum.
art44.why: Once data is abroad, UK law can't follow it unless the paperwork says so. Most US-hosted tools need this.

children.ref: DPA 2018 s.123 and the Children's code
children.name: Children's data
children.says: Services that under-18s use must be designed with their best interests first: high privacy by default, no nudging, clear language, and no profiling unless there's a good reason.
children.why: Children are less able to understand what's happening to their data or push back. The ICO's Age Appropriate Design Code sets out the 15 standards.

duaa.name: The 2025 changes
duaa.says: Updates to UK GDPR: recognised legitimate interests, changes to automated decision-making rules (people must be able to challenge and get a human review), and a complaints procedure.
duaa.why: The DfE checklist for schools follows from this Act. It's why human review and a challenge route appear in the to-do list.
